messages.author: 81e473ecfda78ff0
messages.subject: DSM and stratification by region (habitat)
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have a few questions about stratification in distance sampling and dsm, and would appreciate community input. 

Opening statements: 
1. "Stratification can be used to increase the precision of estimates if we know a priori that density varies between different parts of the study area. As an example, the minke whale data contain two strata: North and South relating to strata further away from and nearer to the Antarctic ice edge, respectively." (Miller et al. 2019 doi: 10.18637/jss.v089.i01).

2. "In design-based sampling, unequal sampling intensity is often accommodated via stratification" (Conn et al. 2017 MEE).

3. (Taken from the minke whale example R script): " When a detection function is fitted to data pooled across strata, the results are actually incorrect because effort was not equally allocated between the strata. The southern stratum is much smaller (84000km2) than the northern (630000km2). But the southern stratum is more desirable habitat for the minke whales.  The southern stratum had much greater survey effort per area than the northern stratum. This is not represented in the pooled analysis." 

Now some questions. Say I want to fit a dsm to the Minke Whale data. My main questions is: "Can I use stratification in (the steps of) a dsm to increase precision?" 

Q1. Is it correct that stratification of the study region will influence the results of the dsm IF stratum is fitted as a covariate in the detection function AND detection varies by stratum? I think it will, as covariates in the detection function are included in the fitted spatial model as an offset to the count (Miller et al 2013). 

Q2. True or false: Stratification will ONLY influence the dsm if detection probability varies by stratum. If detection probability is the same across strata (and thus not included in the detection function) then stratification will not influence the dsm (even if animal densities vary between strata). 

Let's put it all together:
Q3. Assume I want to fit a dsm to minke whale data where: (1) animal densities vary by strata (strata is defined by 3 levels of ice concentration) (2) I have unequal sampling coverage between these strata (3) I have a detection function with equal detection between strata (either because detection function tests indicated this (*opposite to the simulated Minke example data*), or because I have to assume so based on constraints (e.g., too few detections in some strata)).

My own attempt to answer Q3: The dsm itself will not incorporate ''stratification'' in the traditional sense (stratification will not be applicable to increase the precision of estimates, but we expect increased uncertainty where there is low sampling effort). But a dsm is appropriate because "In some sense DSM is a post-stratification, but in the sense that you are explicitly modelling how density changes as a function of the covariates (here ice concentration that would define strata), rather than defining areas over which to estimate density." (copied from one of Dave Miller's answers ("DSM and stratification by year"). 

Thanks in advance for your confirmation/correction/answers on the above questions/statements. 

Chris

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM and stratification by region (habitat)
parts:
Hi Chris, hi listfolk,

For a standard, non-spatial line transect survey, it's often the case
that stratification is recommended to reduce variance. But that variance
reduction comes mostly from a reduction in the encounter rate
uncertainty. I say this because usually encounter rate uncertainty is
larger than detection function uncertainty in line transects and the
driving force in the encounter rate variance is the between-transect
differences. Stratifying tries to put similar transects together (in the
minke example based on high/low density areas), making the per-stratum
variance smaller.

For a density surface model, we have effectively substituted-in the
spatial model in place of the encounter rate variance. This tends to
reduce variance as we're taking into account variation over the whole
study area as a function of environmental covariates (in some sense
taking the continuous version of stratification).

Instead of thinking "stratum covariate in the detection function" we
might be better thinking of this as any other covariate that varies at
the segment level (e.g., Beaufort, wind speed, etc). In this case we can
reduce the detection function variance by including the covariate
(assuming the covariate does explain something about detectability, of
course). This will have the knock-on of reducing the total variance in
your final estimates.

I guess I'd wonder if you have "better" detection covariates than
stratum (which tend to be big) which might have a bigger effect on the
variance (like sighting conditions).

Finally, to your questions:

1. Yes, including a covariate in the detection function will have some
effect on the resulting DSM. What that effect is depends on the
covariate you add, the survey details etc, of course.

2. If detectability is constant, you don't see the effect. I'm not 100%
sure what you mean by "stratification" if there is no covariate in the
detection function. One could include "stratum" in formula for the
spatial model, this would account for density changes (coarsely), which
may be of interest.

3. No question in this one but I'll run with it. Yes, I think your
analysis is correct. As I said above, if you think of your ice
concentration "strata" as an ice concentration covariate, you might find
that this will affect the detectability (more ice==harder to see minkes)
which would be fine as a detection function covariate. Alternatively it
might not be useful and you have a detection function with no/other
covariates. Also fine. The DSM sorts out the unequal coverage issue and
the spatial density changes through the spatial model.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave
